item.title: Discover the top 5 networking errors slowing your home internet
item.itunes:title: Discover the top 5 networking errors slowing your home internet
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Dealing with slow, laggy home Internet is the pits, and it can happen to any home network, from Multi-Gig capable connections to DSL. Even my home network slows down sometimes, and I've got 10GbE for some sections of it. But it's not all about straight-line speeds, with the general responsiveness and reliability of your network being key to a good internet experience. Those things aren't always easy to measure, but simple, quick fixes can get your slow network back to its best.

5 Not putting your router in a central position

The place where your ISP installed your Internet drop is rarely the best place for optimal Wi-Fi

No matter which W-Fi router you have, there's one simple troubleshooting step that should be done before even thinking about upgrades. That's to reposition your router to a more central area in your home, and move it to roughly chest height. That might be tricky depending on where the ISP put your internet hookup, but it's well worth the extra effort on your part.

Okay, maybe two steps, because rebooting your router regularly is a good way to keep your network running smoothly. Also, check for firmware updates if your router isn't new enough to automatically handle that.

New wireless protocols like Wi-Fi 8 are aimed at increasing the stability of your connection, but those routers and access points are some ways away from hitting the market. Plus, they're bound to cost an arm and leg when they finally hit the shelves. But adding a long cable to move your Wi-Fi router from the outside wall the ISP put it on, to somewhere closer to the center of your space will give all your devices a better chance of stable Wi-Fi.

4 Sticking with your ISP's DNS servers

Every (milli)second counts when you're talking about smooth browsing

Your browsing experience is also controlled by the Domain Name Service (DNS), which is often used by your ISP to limit what you can see, or using your DNS query data to sell targeted advertising. Even if they're not doing this (but they probably are), self-hosting a DNS server comes with other benefits, including being able to use local domain names to address your NAS and self-hosted services, ad-blocking at the DNS level, and encrypting your DNS queries for privacy. It's not guaranteed that it will improve your speeds, but it will remove any ISP shenanigans from the equation when set up correctly with DNS-over-TLS, or over-HTTPS, or over-QUIC for encrypting your requests so they can't be read in transit.

3 Interference from too many devices

Especially when you don't have QoS enabled on your router

Despite consumer routers supporting dozens of devices, it's not uncommon to experience slowdowns when you have too many clients trying to hog bandwidth from your router. On a Wi-Fi network alone, you've got typical laptops, consoles, mobiles, and tablets competing for the fixed data capacity, and one untimely update across multiple systems is all it takes for your Internet speeds to plummet. And that's before you include the congestion created by smart gizmos communicating over Bluetooth and other wireless protocols.

Putting bandwidth caps on devices that download GBs of data can give the other systems in your LAN some breathing room. Most consumer routers ship with Quality-of-Service, which allocates a share of their overall bandwidth to high-priority devices. It doesn't really increase the max Internet speed for your local network, but enabling it can help optimize the bandwidth for essential devices.

At the same time, I wouldn't advise going too overboard with QoS or bandwidth caps, or you'll end up with painfully slow Internet speeds on your daily drivers. Likewise, if you have too many IoT devices at 2.4GHz, moving your everyday systems to 5GHz can prevent slowdowns caused by interference.

2 Relying on poorly-placed wireless repeaters

A mesh network is always better for larger households

Switching gears to the hardware side of things, Wi-Fi repeaters may sound nifty for large homes, where you'd get signal drops if you’re too far away from the central router. Unfortunately, their budget-friendly price comes at a massive disadvantage in the form of halved throughput. You see, basic repeaters rely on a single radio chip to receive packets from the router and transmit them to the client devices in a dead zone. Since Wi-Fi can't send and receive packets at the same time, using a cheap wireless repeater can slash the throughput by half. If your repeater creates a new SSID, it can cause your devices to accidentally cling to it, even when they're in range of the central router.

Switching to a mesh setup can fix this problem entirely. Sure, they can be a tad expensive, but if you've got multiple deadzones or want to provide network connectivity over a large zone, it's better to rely on a mesh setup, ideally one with a wired backup to the main router.

1 Using damaged cables or having weak Wi-Fi signals

Networking equipment needs maintenance, just like everything else

Even if you have the fastest networking setup in the world, a broken cable is all it takes to throttle your Internet speeds. I've had copper twisted-pair CAT cable break from tight bends, or from touching sharp edges or the tiny nails on carpet stays, and while fiber is generally quite tough, it can also break from pressure or a tight bend radius. If your internet comes in via coax, it could be physically damaged, or be picking up interference from nearby devices. Check all physical connections for damage, and it's always worth having a few spare cables on hand to test with (or invest in a cable tester).

Wi-Fi signal issues can be harder to pinpoint, but generally they're either caused by being too far from the broadcaster, interference from nearby routers, devices, and your home's walls, or hardware that's not able to keep up anymore. That last point is more likely if your router is older, as they're not built for longevity.

The Internet is a necessity for most households. Don't let yours be slowed by simple mistakes

You don't need an overkill home network setup or prosumer hardware to keep your home internet running smoothly. Most simple mistakes can be fixed with simple troubleshooting, and you'll be back at your expected speeds in no time. It's generally a better idea to upgrade your router before thinking about moving to a higher tier on your internet plan, as newer routers have better features overall, and you might not notice the increased ISP plan without it.

item.title: I finally set up Windows File History properly, and it saved a folder I'd deleted twice
item.itunes:title: I finally set up Windows File History properly, and it saved a folder I'd deleted twice
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Windows backup tools don’t get the same appreciation as third-party alternatives. Microsoft has decided to permanently retire the old Backup and Restore tool, and you might not find it in future OS builds. Since Microsoft consolidated its efforts around promoting the new Windows Backup tool, the older tools have received far less attention. There are a couple more options apart from Windows Backup, and one of them is File History.

This rarely used Windows backup tool launched with Windows 8 as a specialized solution for maintaining multiple versions of your files and folders. But I didn’t use it because a more comprehensive system backup solution made sense. However, none of those tools could maintain multiple copies (versions) of the same files, and after I began using File History, it helped me recover files and folders that would otherwise be gone for good.

Accidental deletions are unavoidable

File History saved me from one

My Windows PC is a cluttered mess, and I put off minor cleanups and organization for later. You can call it laziness, which is an apt term for a user who always finds an excuse for anything maintenance-related on their computer. My downloads and document folders are very precious to me, and I don't use OneDrive on my main PC. I only use it on test virtual machines when I need to spot a new feature or play with the settings.

I set up File History at the beginning of July, a couple of months ago, as a precaution to back up these folders. Before that, I periodically copied the files to another drive and an external drive as a preventive measure. Last month was tax season in my country, and that meant dealing with bank statements, client invoices, and other tax portal documents, all of which were necessary for an accurate tax filing. I gathered all these documents, filed the tax return, and then didn't check them again until after the deadline.

I tested 8 File Explorer alternatives, but this is the one that stuck

File Pilot is the king

24
By  João Carrasqueira

One fine day, my C drive was almost full, and I needed to make space for a couple of ISO files. So I frantically deleted a large chunk of images, documents, archives, and folders from Downloads without checking those useful PDFs, then emptied the Recycle Bin as well. A week later, I needed one of the invoices and a bank account statement to modify the filing, and I couldn’t find them or the parent folder. I panicked for a few minutes before realizing that File History had been saving and preserving versions of these folders.

Restoring previous versions is a fascinating feature

Bringing back deleted items

I right-clicked on the folder, opened its properties, and switched to the Previous Versions tab. It showed me the option to restore everything in that folder, and with a few clicks, my documents were restored in the Downloads folder. The best thing about the feature is that it can preserve multiple versions of the same folder or file. This lets you browse and restore very old versions of an Excel or Word fileyou overwrote as the project progressed.

Another way to browse versions is through the File History interface, which you can launch directly from the Properties window. The interface offers an easy carousel format to view available versions and restore the one you want. I like the fact that File History doesn't encrypt files or make them unreadable on other machines. You can browse the external drive directly to find the files, and it even works on another system.

But browsing the external hard drive directly takes longer, since you can't choose the backup version you need. The folder shows all the files backed up to the drive, but lacks version-selection and restoration controls. Also, you must configure File History beforehand to avoid sticky situations like the one I faced a few weeks back.

Fine-tuning version frequency

Covering all the bases

File History’s most impressive feature is that it saves and maintains versions indefinitely, unless you specify otherwise. There are niche use cases where this approach makes sense. For example, consider a user like me who has maybe 2–3 GB of files in the Downloads and Documents folders. The total size is very small compared to the target driveFile History uses to maintain thebackup.

Even if I set the save frequency to every ten minutes, it’ll take a long time to fill the drive. File History only maintains versions of files that are mutable, like a text file or another such editable document. It tracks changes to the file, creates a new copy, and backs up any new files added after the last session. So, it doesn't duplicate files except the ones you modified.

Robocopy is still the fastest way to copy thousands of files on Windows, and I wasted years not using it

Discover the hidden power of Robocopy, a CLI tool that offers lightning-fast file copying and greater control over your copy sessions.

1
By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

You can choose to stick to the default one-hour cycle or increase the save frequency to daily or even as low as ten minutes. Apart from the usual external drive option, you can choose a network drive for backup as well. I prefer the physical drive option as it remains connected to the system and mounts when I boot to the desktop. There’s no need to repeat the connection or setup, as File History scans for the drive, tracks changes, and initiates backup automatically.

Protect your files

File History is not a traditional backup tool that can back up the complete system. It’s a leaner, hyper-specific tool to back up files and maintain multiple versions of select locations. I wouldn’t suggest using it to back up very large folders, and instead save only the Library and a few other locations on other drives. File History is completely free, doesn’t need a Microsoft account to work, and all these traits make it an indispensable tool for Windows users. However, it needs a facelift and maybe a separate app or a section in the Settings app, as Microsoft is slowly phasing out the Control Panel.

item.title: Valve’s Left 4 Dead 2 team leaked its own trailer after the ESRB blocked its release
item.itunes:title: Valve’s Left 4 Dead 2 team leaked its own trailer after the ESRB blocked its release
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Valve leaked the Left 4 Dead 2 trailer themselves to sidestep ESRB restrictions.
  • ESRB demands forced Valve to tone down in-game lines and cut drug/alcohol references.
  • The leak blurs whether some "leaks" are real or staged to dodge rules or drum up hype.

If you were PC gaming around October 2009, you may remember that someone leaked the Left 4 Dead 2 trailer online. At the time, it felt like perhaps Valve was furious that someone had managed to leak data ahead of the game's release. However, it turns out that Valve held the cards the whole time, as the lead for Left 4 Dead 2 admitted that the company uploaded it themselves to dodge ESRB rulings.

Left 4 Dead 2's project lead admits Valve leaked the trailer itself

The ESRB wouldn't allow it any other way

Over on his YouTube channel, the project lead and writer for Left 4 Dead 2, Chet Faliszek, discussed what went on behind the scenes when writing the characters. I highly recommend watching the entire video and not just skipping to the part where he admits that Valve leaked its own trailer. It's a fascinating insight into how he wrote the characters, why some lines got cut from the final product, and the struggles he faced.

One of those struggles was trying to appease the ESRB, the board behind giving the game an age rating. To achieve the rating Valve wanted for the first Left 4 Dead title, Faliszek had to cut lines from the game that the ESRB didn't like. This included references to drugs and alcohol, including Faliszek's favorite line from Francis during the Dead Air campaign. It would have had Francis remark, "This is the most sober I've ever been in an airport," but it was cut due to the alcohol reference.

When making Left 4 Dead 2, Valve butted heads once more with the ESRB. One of the pain points was with the trailer, which the ESRB wanted changed before it was officially released. Valve didn't want to change it, so they instead took the unofficial route:

"...especially for Left 4 Dead 2, with the ESRB, we...we leaked the ES—we leaked our trailer ahead of time, because they wouldn't let us release the trailer. I'll just admit that, I think we can't get in trouble for that now. It's like 20 years ago.

Um, so it's funny seeing leaked stuff now because, yeah, you can't look—I don't think you can look for 'leaked Left 4 Dead 2 trailer' because it's just going to be, eh, it's lost now. But yeah, it originally got leaked because we—we had this with the ESRB, and so that's why, like a lot of the language got to get toned down..."

It does make me wonder how many leaks in the gaming industry were legitimate leaks and how many were the company deliberately trying to skirt under rules or generate hype. Still, it's good that the story behind Left 4 Dead 2's trailer came to light.

item.title: Your Windows 11 PC uploads your update files by default, but one setting controls where they go
item.itunes:title: Your Windows 11 PC uploads your update files by default, but one setting controls where they go
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For all the things it does right, Windows 11 also has a pesky habit of making decisions for you that you don't necessarily remember agreeing to. Some are harmless enough, while others quietly change how your PC behaves in the background. Somewhere in the middle of these two areas falls Delivery Optimization. Microsoft designed it to make Windows updates faster and more efficient by allowing your PC to get update files from other computers instead of relying entirely on Microsoft's servers.

The catch, however, is that this works both ways. Peer-to-peer sharing is enabled by default. On current versions of Windows, it means that your PC can share update data with other devices on your local network. It won't, by default, upload Microsoft's updates to random PCs on the internet, but there's a separate setting that allows it to do exactly that. Microsoft doesn't get to rummage through your personal files, but this feature does use your bandwidth to help deliver its updates to someone else.

I’m a power user and I’m disabling these Windows features on purpose

If you've used Windows 11 for any length of time, you'll understand.

8
By  Korbin Brown

Delivery Optimization isn't quite what you think

Your PC isn't sharing your personal files

Delivery Optimization is Microsoft's peer-to-peer system for getting Windows updates onto PCs without making every machine pull everything directly from Microsoft's servers. Windows can download pieces of an update from Microsoft's CDN (content delivery network) and other eligible peers at the same time. That is particularly useful when millions of PCs are all trying to update at once. On paper, this means fewer trips to Microsoft's own servers, leading to less congestion and potentially faster downloads — "potentially" being the operative word here.

Almost a decade ago, Microsoft had automatically made it so that your updates could be shared with peers on the internet on Windows 10 Home and Pro versions, but that is no longer the case. On Windows 11, this is an entirely opt-in feature, and even then, it doesn't mean that your OS becomes a mini torrent client for your hard drive. Delivery Optimization deals with update content, and not documents, photos, games, or that folder named "Study Material." The downloaded pieces are also vetted before Windows uses them, so a corrupted or tampered-with chunk isn't accepted just because another PC sent it.

So far, this sounds fairly sensible — and it is. The interesting bit is who Windows considers an "eligible peer" because "other devices" can mean something considerably narrower than the internet at large. That's where the setting most people never touch becomes important.

This dinosaur machine now runs my LLMs inside an LXC

4
By  Ayush Pande

The setting, by default, is a lot less dramatic than you might think

Just check where your PC is allowed to share

On current versions of Windows, Delivery Optimization's peer-to-peer functionality is enabled by default, but there's an important catch: the default is LAN-only. In other words, your PC can exchange update data with eligible devices on your local network, not random computers belonging to strangers somewhere on the internet. The setting Microsoft documents as the default is "Devices on my local network."

Now, Windows does offer a "Devices on the internet and my local network" option, and that is what can expand peer sharing beyond your network. This is the setting you should check if you don't want your PC to participate in Microsoft's wider peer-to-peer network. Even if you might not have turned this on by default, it's possible for organizational policies or an older configuration to change this default behavior and turn it on.

Still, there is a solid reason to turn peer sharing off entirely, even if it's restricted to the local network. A single-PC household has little to gain from sharing updates with other devices on the same network, while anyone with a restrictive upload allowance may prefer not to donate bandwidth they could otherwise be using.

I’m a power user and I’m disabling these Windows features on purpose

If you've used Windows 11 for any length of time, you'll understand.

8
By  Korbin Brown

How to take control of Delivery Optimization

Check the setting before you blame your bandwidth

Firstly, head to Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Delivery Optimization. Here, look for "Allow downloads from other devices." If you want peer-to-peer sharing gone entirely, turn it off completely. But if you don't mind sharing with PCs on your own local network, you can leave it enabled. Just make sure that "Devices on my local network" is the option you've selected. The internet option is the one to avoid if you don't want your PC exchanging update data with machines outside your network.

For anyone who prefers numbers to reassuring toggles, Microsoft's underlying modes make the distinction clearer. 0 means Microsoft only, 1 means local network, 2 means a local Group, and 3 means internet plus local network. Current Windows installations use Mode 1 by default, so seeing the toggle enabled doesn't automatically mean your PC is uploading to the internet.

Group Policy Editor is only available if you are running a Windows Pro, Enterprise, or Education edition.

You can also control the Delivery Optimization settings of your version of Windows through Group Policy, where the DownloadMode registry value exposes the same underlying setting. That's useful if you want the choice enforced rather than trusting that nobody will change it later. Search for "group policy" in the Windows Start menu, and click on "Edit group policy." Head to Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Delivery Optimization > Download Mode to see what yours is set to.

And there's a simple way to see what Windows is actually doing: open Delivery Optimization > Activity Monitor. It shows download and upload activity, including peer traffic. If the internet upload figures are empty, you have nothing to worry about, since it means that your PC is sitting comfortably in the LAN-only default.

The default definitely deserves a second look sometimes

It's always a good idea to know where these settings and their toggles are on your PC.

Settings like these aren't necessarily malicious, invasive, or unreasonable. They are just decisions made on your behalf until you have a reason to wonder what your PC is actually doing. They're easy to ignore, and especially so when everything appears to work exactly as it should.

This, in no way, means that you need to hunt down and disable every Windows background feature immediately, either. However, it's always a good idea to know what these switches control and where they are on your PC. And when a setting involves your network, your bandwidth, or your hardware doing work you didn't realize it was doing, having the choice to turn it off is definitely worth the few seconds it takes to check.

item.itunes:summary:
Building a simple webpage with AI isn’t hard anymore, but making it look polished and intentional is a different story. It’s easy for a model to generate working code; it’s much harder for it to balance margins, pick the right contrast, and keep every visual element aligned.

item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra as the start of what it hopes will be its "AGI era"
item.itunes:title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra as the start of what it hopes will be its "AGI era"
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • OpenAI unveils GPT-6 Astra: most capable model, rated "Critical" for cybersecurity.
  • OpenAI explains that GPT-6 Astra is also the safest and most secure model it has made.
  • OpenAI says Astra is more robust and safer than GPT-5.6 Sol, and may usher in the AGI era.

Today has been a wild day for AI news. Earlier today, we saw Nvidia announce that it's acquiring Hugging Face for a cool $12.93 billion, promising to keep the open-source nature of the platform alive. Now, OpenAI has revealed GPT-6 Astra, the model the company hopes will deliver AGI to everyone

OpenAI pulls back the curtain on GPT-6 Astra

Plus, everything it's doing to keep it from flying off the rails

You can check out all the details of GPT-6 Astra on its system card. OpenAI calls it "the most capable model we have ever broadly deployed," and, somewhat scarily, it's the first AI model to reach "Critical " level when it comes to cybersecurity capability. OpenAI explains what that means in more tangible terms:

"This means that, with the right tools and access, GPT-6 Astra can find previously unknown security flaws and develop new ways to exploit them across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step. Accordingly, we significantly strengthened our protections against the model taking harmful cyber actions, whether that’s due to misuse or misalignment."

While OpenAI is keen to show off how mighty its new model is, a considerable amount of the first section is dedicated to the company telling us how it'll keep it from breaking out. It says GPT-6 Astra is "significantly more robust than its predecessors," which means it's a lot harder for people to crack it open and tell it to do things against the terms of use. It's also "better aligned than GPT-5.6 Sol," which means it will keep itself more aligned with OpenAI's safety rules than its prior model. Overall, OpenAI claims that GPT-6 Astra is "significantly safer" than GPT-5.6 Sol in high-risk situations, which is reassuring to hear, given how mighty this new model seems to be.

OpenAI seems to believe that this model will be the one to achieve the legendary goal of reaching Artificial General Intelligence, or AGI. This is when an AI begins working and thinking like a human, and has been the holy grail for AI companies ever since LLMs hit the scene. In an interview reported by Wired, OpenAI President and cofounder Greg Brockman says he feels pretty confident:

“It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era. I think that if we fast-forward a couple of years, when we look back and say, ‘When was it really that AGI was created?’ I think it's going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model."

item.title: UGREEN's new smart home platform keeps your AI and storage local, no cloud required
item.itunes:title: UGREEN's new smart home platform keeps your AI and storage local, no cloud required
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • HomeAgent merges local storage, AI, security, and device control into a single smart-home hub.
  • MasterAgent MA100 uses Nvidia Jetson Thor for heavy local AI, runs larger models and developer extensions.
  • Local-first design emphasizes privacy and on-device searches, while some cloud services remain optional.

UGREEN is moving well beyond chargers, docks, and network-attached storage. At its Smart Living Launch Event at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, which I attended on Sept. 1, the company introduced HomeAgent, a new smart home platform built around local storage and AI processing. This marks UGREEN’s first serious foray into AIoT, and the scope is broader than I expected. The lineup ranges from compact HomeAgent hubs to security cameras, a smart speaker, smart displays, and a much more powerful Nvidia Jetson-based system.

UGREEN wants HomeAgent to become your smart home's local brain

The HA100 combines storage, AI, security, and device control

  • Credit: Source: UGREEN
  • Credit: Source: UGREEN

The HomeAgent HA100 and HA100 Pro are the center of the ecosystem and the products that make UGREEN's overall pitch easiest to understand. Instead of treating local storage, smart home control, and AI as separate components, HomeAgent combines them into a single box. Files, photos, security footage, and device activity can all be stored locally, while supported AI processing also happens on the device. UGREEN says the core storage, file management, security, and smart home functions can operate over the local network without a monthly storage fee.

Building a local smart home is easy until you try to replace the speaker

I replaced everything with local-only hardware, but this was the most difficult.

4
By  Rich Edmonds

That matters because this isn't being positioned as just another Matter hub with a few extra features attached. The HA100 is designed to handle storage, security, computing, and device control together, giving UGREEN a very different starting point from companies that began with bulbs, plugs, or cameras. Matter support enables compatible devices to be integrated into a single system, allowing users to build automation scenes and coordinate multiple devices. It can also search recorded security footage using keywords, which is the kind of feature that makes local AI more useful than simply slapping an "AI" label on the box.

UGREEN is also bringing its Uliya voice assistant into the platform. Uliya can control supported devices, check live status or event history, and create voice notifications for things such as a package arriving or a baby crying. The HA100 Pro takes that further with faster networking and improved AI performance, including advanced recognition, contextual device control, and voice-based automation rule creation. That's where the distinction between the regular and Pro models starts to become more meaningful than a basic performance bump.

MasterAgent pushes UGREEN's local AI plans much further

Nvidia's Jetson Thor gives the MA100 serious processing power

The MasterAgent MA100 is where UGREEN's ambitions get much bigger. The company describes it as an agentic AI local hub built around Nvidia's Jetson Thor T5000 platform, with up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS of local compute performance. That's far beyond what most people would expect from a conventional smart-home hub, making the MA100 feel less like an accessory and more like a dedicated local AI appliance.

UGREEN says the added performance will let MasterAgent run larger models locally, understand more complex context and intent, and coordinate multiple devices and tasks around the home. Developers will also be able to extend it with packages or skills. That developer angle is important because a box this powerful makes more sense if UGREEN can build a broader software ecosystem around it rather than limiting it to a fixed set of first-party functions.

The rest of the announced hardware fills out the devices around those hubs. UGREEN showed the SynCare Indoor Cam ID500 Pro, SynCare PoE Cam OD600 Pro, SynCare Battery Cam OD800 Pro, Smart Speaker for Uliya, and UGREEN Gallery. Gallery includes LCD smart frames that can display photos and AI-generated highlight videos from a user's local library. Taken together, the lineup makes it clear that UGREEN isn’t testing the smart-home market with a single standalone device. It's trying to launch the pieces of an ecosystem at once.

UGREEN is betting that local AI can differentiate its ecosystem

Privacy and useful automation are central to the pitch

The part of UGREEN's strategy I find most interesting is that local processing isn't treated as a side feature. It's the foundation of the system. HomeAgent can recognize people, vehicles, pets, and packages, summarize events, surface unusual activity, and search through recorded footage. At the same time, the same platform can work with personal photos and videos stored at home. That's a much more practical use of local AI than simply adding another chatbot to a smart-home app.

The part of UGREEN's strategy I find most interesting is that local processing isn't being treated as a side feature.

There are still cloud dependencies, and UGREEN is explicit about that. Account registration and authentication, remote access, mobile notifications, software updates, and optional cloud-enabled services may still require an internet connection or cloud services. So "local-first" shouldn't be read as "completely offline." The important distinction is that UGREEN is keeping core storage, device control, and supported AI workloads in-home rather than making cloud processing the default for everything.

The launch also expands UGREEN's existing relationship with the New England Patriots. The company named Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez its Global Brand Ambassador after becoming the team's Official Tech Accessory Partner earlier this year. "Just like UGREEN, I believe great technology should help people stay prepared, reach their potential, and bring their A-game in the moments that matter most," Gonzalez said during the announcement.

Preorders for the HomeAgent HA100, HA100 Pro, and MasterAgent MA100 open Sept.3 through UGREEN's AIoT store, ahead of a Kickstarter campaign scheduled for Oct. 27. Customers can place a deposit of $50 to secure the Super Early Bird price, advertised at 50% off. Additional AIoT accessories are expected to join the campaign when it launches. The bigger question now isn't whether UGREEN wants into the smart-home market. It's whether this local-first approach can give people a reason to build around HomeAgent instead of adding yet another disconnected hub to what they already have.

item.title: I turned my old Galaxy phone into a gaming PC with Samsung DeX and one hidden feature
item.itunes:title: I turned my old Galaxy phone into a gaming PC with Samsung DeX and one hidden feature
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Consumer hardware is getting more expensive by the day due to rising AI demand and the enormous amount of compute it requires. Resources such as RAM are becoming increasingly scarce for consumers, so we have to make the most of the hardware we already have.

I've already been trying to make the most of an old laptop I had lying around, turning it into one of the most important devices in my home. I also had an old Samsung Galaxy S21 FE lying around, which is now nearly five years old. I wanted to do something useful with the smartphone and eventually turned it into a gaming beast.

"Beast" is a strong word for a mid-premium smartphone, but when I paired the Galaxy S21 FE with Samsung's DeX and Game Native and connected it to a TV, it actually lived up to that description.

The Samsung Galaxy gaming setup

Never thought I'd write these words

Samsung DeX already lets you connect a compatible Galaxy phone to a television and use Android apps through a desktop-style interface. GameNative adds the more interesting part by allowing Windows games from Steam, Epic Games, and GOG to run locally on the phone.

GameNative relies on several translation layers before a Windows game can run on Android. It uses Wine or Proton to run Windows applications, and a CPU translator to convert x86 or x64 instructions for the phone's ARM processor. Tools such as DXVK or VKD3D then translate DirectX graphics calls into Vulkan. The Galaxy GPU renders the final image, and DeX displays it on the television.

I was able to run the setup comfortably on the Galaxy S21 FE, which means it should also run well on any newer Galaxy S series and Z series phones. The phone also needs a USB-C dock because its single port has to handle HDMI output, power, and wired accessories simultaneously. You are also going to need a 45W or 65W PPS charger and, if you really want to make the most of this setup, an Xbox controller, a PlayStation controller, or another compatible XInput controller.

The Pixel's desktop mode feels like a real operating system, and it's already better than I expected

I don't know when I'd actually use the Pixel's desktop mode, but it's surprisingly polished despite its lackluster third-party app support.

6
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Setting up DeX and getting the performance right

This takes some effort

For gaming, a wired DeX connection is the better option because wireless DeX adds compression and input delay. I connected a charger to the USB-C dock, ran HDMI from the dock to the TV, and then plugged in the Galaxy S21 FE. I kept DeX at 1920×1080 pixels and 60Hz, since pushing 4K only adds more load and many docks or TVs drop to 30Hz at that resolution.

The TV also needs Game Mode enabled, with motion smoothing and other image-processing features turned off to reduce latency. Once DeX is running, the phone's display can stay off. In Game Booster, I used the Performance profile. On supported devices, the optional "Pause USB PD charging when gaming" setting can also help reduce heat by limiting battery charging during gameplay.

For GameNative, 1280 × 720 at 30fps is a good starting point for demanding games on the S21 FE. You can push lighter titles to higher resolutions once they are stable. I would only change the renderer, graphics driver, or DirectX wrapper if a game has compatibility or performance issues. LSFG frame generation can make a stable 30 fps output look closer to 60 fps, but it works best as a finishing touch after the game is already running smoothly.

How well does it actually run games?

It's pretty impressive

My Galaxy S21 FE is the Snapdragon 888 model with 8GB of RAM, and the results were better than I expected from a phone this old.

It goes without saying that this setup really shines in lighter games. For example, Dead Cells runs extremely well and is almost ideal for something like this because it already works perfectly with a controller and doesn't put much pressure on the hardware. Portal 2 was another surprisingly good experience. Once you're sitting on the couch with the game running through DeX on a television, it doesn't feel like you're playing a Windows game on an old Android phone.

However, titles such as The Witcher 3, Cyberpunk 2077, and Red Dead Redemption 2 push the Snapdragon 888 to its limits, so this is where you can lower the resolution and target a stable 30fps. You're obviously not getting the same experience as with a modern gaming PC or console, but the fact that games of this scale can run locally on the S21 FE at all makes the setup impressive.

Heat is the biggest issue I encountered – the S21 FE already has a reputation for running hot, and my unit has heated up considerably even during normal use over the years, so gaming only makes things worse.

I wouldn't use the S21 FE as a replacement for a gaming PC or console. But for an old phone that was otherwise sitting idle, being able to play Dead Cells, Portal 2, and even experiment with games like Cyberpunk 2077 on a television gives it a remarkably useful second life.

The future of Android-powered TV streaming sticks looks uncertain

The Google TV Streamer was released in 2024 and the future of something new isn't clear.

4
By  Brian Burgess

item.title: I used Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini to build a resume, but only one felt interview-ready
item.itunes:title: I used Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini to build a resume, but only one felt interview-ready
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
While some people use AI to write entire documents or completely replace their work, this opens you up to problems like hallucinations and generic output. The real value of AI tools lies in using them as collaborative partners that can help you identify blind spots and speed up repetitive processes.

So recently, when a friend needed help with the resume, but both of us were struggling with the planning stage, I decided to try out Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini to get some insights on how to approach the document.

I gave Claude Code control of my desktop for a week, and it automated things I didn't think were possible

I was seriously stunned.

59
By  Simon Batt

Why use AI for help with a resume?

Leveraging AI's strengths while retaining control

In this particular scenario, AI was the perfect tool to help me craft the resume. My friend has some old experience as a paramedic and currently works in sales. However, he has no tertiary education besides his ambulance certificate. At the same time, he works 50 hours a week and struggles to find the time to actually work on maintaining the documents for his new job search.

I offered to help, but knew how time-consuming it can be to format and structure a CV. Since I don't work in the sales industry, I also wasn't sure how to translate his experience into a compelling profile.

I knew that AI could help us in multiple ways. It would identify the blind spots I have when it comes to translating his experience, and it would speed up the process of crafting and structuring the document. At the same time, I made sure to steer away from using AI for the cover letter or to write the entire resume — I just needed it to provide the structure and some questions to address.

All the tools found a way to transfer seemingly unrelated skills

There's no clear winner in this area

My decision to turn to AI immediately yielded some useful insights. I started out by providing each tool with a quick summary of my friend's context. I also asked about what questions he should address in the resume. While I wasn't sure how to translate my friend's past experience as a paramedic into something relevant to his current job search, each AI tool could.

Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude all noted that while this experience isn't directly relevant, it can be highlighted in terms of skills and what the job taught him. This included skills like working under pressure, remaining calm in stressful situations, and being reliable.
